docs.title: VisualLLM - Visual Question Answering
docs.text:
This repository explores Visual Question Answering (VQA) using Large Language Models without explicit fine-tuning. The project investigates how different pipeline configurations combining vision models (BLIP, YOLO) with LLMs (Llama-2, Mistral) perform on VQA tasks through prompt engineering and in-context learning.This will be helpful for improving image search and recommendation systems.

Institution: Northeastern University Focus Areas: Visual Question Answering, Multi-modal AI, Prompt Engineering, In-Context Learning

docs.title: Research Context
docs.text:
This project was developed as part of coursework exploring modern approaches to multi-modal AI. The work demonstrates:

✅ Zero-shot VQA - Answer visual questions without task-specific training ✅ Pipeline modularity - Mix and match vision + language components ✅ Prompt engineering - Optimize LLM performance through careful prompting ✅ In-context learning - Leverage few-shot examples for improved accuracy ✅ Comparative analysis - Systematic evaluation of different approaches

docs.title: What is Visual Question Answering?
docs.text:
Visual Question Answering (VQA) is the challenging task of answering natural language questions about images. The model must understand both the visual content and the question to generate accurate answers.

Examples:

Question Image Answer How many children are in bed? 2 Who is wearing glasses? Man Is the umbrella upside down? Yes

This is particularly significant for making LLMs truly multi-modal and enabling them to process and reason about visual information.

docs.text: This research project has main aspects of pipeline performance exploration for the task of VQA which can be used to improve image search and recommendation systems.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BLIP + LLM pipeline combines image captioning capabilities with large language models to perform Visual Question Answering (VQA). This approach leverages BLIP (Bootstrapping Language and Image Pre-training) to generate descriptive captions of images, which are then used as context for LLMs (Llama-2 or Mistral) to answer questions about the images.

docs.title: 1. BLIP Image Captioning
docs.text:
BLIP (Bootstrapping Language and Image Pre-training) is a flexible framework designed specifically for image captioning tasks. When provided with an image, BLIP outputs a descriptive caption by:

  • Processing the input image through a patch embedding layer
  • Using a transformer encoder to understand relationships between image patches
  • Generating a word sequence through a language decoder

Model Used: BLIP-1 pre-trained on COCO dataset

Example Output: - Input: Image of children sleeping - Output: "Children are sleeping calmly in bed"

docs.title: 2. Prompt Construction
docs.text: The pipeline constructs prompts by combining: 1. BLIP-generated caption 2. User's question 3. Specific instructions for answer format

docs.title: 3. LLM Processing
docs.text: Two LLM variants are supported: - Llama-2-7b-chat-hf: Meta's conversational model - Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2: Mistral AI's instruction-following model

docs.title: BLIP + Llama Configuration
docs.text: The pipeline processes images by: 1. Loading question-answer pairs and pre-generated BLIP captions 2. Combining the datasets for unified processing 3. Initializing the Llama-2 text generation model on available hardware (CUDA/CPU) 4. Authenticating with HuggingFace for model access

docs.title: BLIP + Mistral Configuration
docs.text: The pipeline similarly processes images using: 1. The same data loading approach as Llama 2. Mistral text generation model configured for optimal performance 3. Automatic hardware detection and memory optimization

docs.title: Prompt Templates
docs.text: The pipeline implements four different prompt configurations, progressively increasing in complexity:

docs.title: Configuration 1: Default (20 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Baseline performance with minimal constraints

The prompt combines the BLIP caption with the question and generates up to 20 tokens for the answer.

Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): 'Children are sleeping in bed',
Answer the question 'How many children are there?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 2: Token-Limited (3 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Restrict output length to improve answer quality

This configuration uses the same prompt structure as Configuration 1 but limits the output to a maximum of 3 tokens, encouraging more concise answers.

docs.title: Configuration 3: Token-Limited + Prompt Restriction
docs.text:
Purpose: Combine token limit with explicit single-word instruction

The prompt includes an explicit instruction to "Answer in a single word" combined with the 3-token limit, providing both generation constraints and prompt-level guidance.

Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): 'Children are sleeping in bed'.
Answer in a single word the question: 'How many children are there?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 4: Enhanced Prompt (Best Performance)
docs.text:
Purpose: Comprehensive instructions to ensure clean, single-word answers

This configuration adds detailed instructions specifying: - Use plain English without emoticons, icons, or special formatting - Provide only the answer without repeating the question or adding explanations - Answer in lowercase single word format - Return 'NA' if unable to answer based on the caption - Limited to 3 tokens maximum

Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): 'Children are sleeping in bed'.
Answer in a single word the question: 'How many children are there?'
In plain simple English language without any emoticons or icons or font colors or punctuation marks.
I strongly state do not repeat the question, prompt used, disclaimer, explanation or anything apart from answer,
that is just provide the answer in a single word in lowercase, the question: 'How many children are there?'.
Remember if you are unable to answer the question based on the caption provided by BLIP, mention 'NA'.
Answer:

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Image → BLIP Captioning → Prompt Construction → LLM Inference → Answer Extraction
  1. Load Data: Question-answer pairs + pre-generated BLIP captions
  2. Initialize Model: Load LLM (Llama/Mistral) on CUDA/CPU
  3. Generate Answers: For each image-question pair, construct prompt from caption and generate response
  4. Save Results: Store outputs (image ID, caption, question, prompt, answer) to CSV files

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
1. Descriptive Context: BLIP captions provide natural language descriptions that capture the overall scene
  2. Simple Pipeline: Straightforward architecture with only two main components
  3. Good for Scene Understanding: Effective for questions about overall image content and atmosphere
  4. Fast Inference: Minimal preprocessing required before LLM processing

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. Numerical Questions: Caption may not include specific counts
  2. Example: "Children sleeping in bed" doesn't specify how many children
  3. Object Details: May miss specific objects not central to the scene
  4. Spatial Relationships: Limited ability to answer precise location questions
  5. Caption Quality Dependency: Performance heavily relies on BLIP's caption accuracy

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
Best suited for: - Questions about scene description ("What is happening in the image?") - Mood/atmosphere queries ("What is the emotion shown?") - General content questions ("What type of room is this?") - Activity recognition ("What are people doing?")

Not recommended for: - Precise counting questions ("How many objects?") - Detailed object detection ("What specific items are visible?") - Spatial arrangement queries ("Where is object X relative to Y?")

docs.title: BLIP + YOLO + LLM Hybrid Pipeline Architecture
Overview
docs.text:
The BLIP + YOLO + LLM hybrid pipeline combines the strengths of both image captioning and object detection to provide comprehensive visual context for Large Language Models. This approach leverages:

  • BLIP for high-level scene understanding and descriptive captions
  • YOLO for precise object detection and counting
  • LLM (Llama-2 or Mistral) for question answering with enriched context

This hybrid architecture achieves the best overall semantic match accuracy (0.6423 for Llama) by providing both holistic scene understanding and detailed object-level information.

docs.title: 1. Parallel Processing: BLIP + YOLO
docs.text:
The hybrid pipeline processes images through both models:

BLIP Contribution: - High-level scene description - Context about overall image content - Implicit mood, activity, and atmosphere

YOLO Contribution: - Explicit object enumeration - Object counts and presence - Structured object information

Example: - BLIP: "Children are sleeping calmly in bed" - YOLO: "person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89), pillow (0.82), pillow (0.80)" - Combined: Provides both scene understanding AND precise object counts

docs.title: 2. Context Merging Strategy
docs.text:
The pipeline combines both information sources into a unified prompt:

Caption: {BLIP_caption}
Detections: {YOLO_detections}
Question: {user_question}

This dual-context approach enables the LLM to: - Use caption for scene understanding questions - Use detections for counting/object questions - Cross-reference both for comprehensive answers

docs.title: 3. LLM Processing
docs.text: Two LLM variants are supported: - Llama-2-7b-chat-hf: Best overall performance (Semantic: 0.6423) - Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2: Competitive performance with proper prompting

docs.title: BLIP + YOLO + Llama Configuration
docs.text: The hybrid pipeline processes images by: 1. Clearing GPU cache for optimal memory management 2. Loading pre-computed data containing both BLIP captions and YOLO detections 3. Initializing the Llama-2 text generation model on available hardware 4. Authenticating with HuggingFace for model access

docs.title: BLIP + YOLO + Mistral Configuration
docs.text: The pipeline similarly processes images using: 1. GPU cache management for efficient processing 2. Loading the same pre-computed dual-context data (captions and detections) 3. Mistral text generation model configured with optimized data types 4. Automatic hardware detection and configuration

docs.title: Prompt Templates
docs.text: The hybrid pipeline implements four configurations combining both caption and detection information:

docs.title: Configuration 1: Default (20 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Baseline with dual-context

The prompt combines both BLIP caption and YOLO detections with the question, generating up to 20 tokens for the answer. This provides the LLM with comprehensive visual context from both sources.

Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): Children are sleeping in bed,
and Object detections (generated by YOLOv5): person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89),
Answer the question 'How many children are there?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 2: Token-Limited (3 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Restrict output for concise answers

This configuration uses the same dual-context prompt structure as Configuration 1 but limits the output to a maximum of 3 tokens, encouraging more focused and concise responses.

docs.title: Configuration 3: Token-Limited + Prompt Restriction
docs.text:
Purpose: Combine token limit with single-word instruction

The prompt includes an explicit instruction to "Answer in a single word" combined with the 3-token limit and dual context from both BLIP and YOLO, providing comprehensive information with strict output constraints.

Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): 'Children are sleeping in bed',
and Object detections (generated by YOLOv5): person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89).
Answer in a single word the question: 'How many children are there?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 4: Enhanced Prompt (Best Performance)
docs.text:
Purpose: Comprehensive instructions with dual context

This configuration adds detailed instructions specifying: - Leverage both BLIP caption and YOLO detections for comprehensive context - Use plain English without emoticons, icons, or special formatting - Provide only the answer without repeating the question or adding explanations - Answer in lowercase single word format - Return 'NA' if unable to answer based on the provided information - Limited to 3 tokens maximum

Complete Example: 

Based on the image caption (generated by BLIP model): 'Children are sleeping calmly in bed'
and Object detections (generated by YOLOv5): 'person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89), pillow (0.82)'.
Answer in a single word the question: 'How many children are there?'
In plain simple English language without any emoticons or icons or font colors or punctuation marks.
I strongly state do not repeat the question, prompt used, disclaimer, explanation or anything apart from answer,
that is just provide the answer in a single word in lowercase, the question: 'How many children are there?'.
Remember if you are unable to answer the question based on the caption provided by BLIP, mention 'NA'.
Answer:

docs.title: 1. Comprehensive Context
docs.text:
• Scene Understanding: BLIP provides holistic description
  • Object Details: YOLO provides precise object information
  • Redundancy Benefits: Multiple information sources improve reliability

docs.title: 2. Question Type Coverage
docs.text: Handles diverse question categories: - Counting: "How many X?" → Use YOLO detections - Scene Description: "What's happening?" → Use BLIP caption - Object Presence: "Is there a Y?" → Use both sources - Activity Recognition: "What are they doing?" → Use BLIP caption - Attribute Queries: Best effort with both sources

docs.title: 3. Best Semantic Understanding
docs.text:
• Achieves 0.6423 semantic match (highest across all pipelines)
  • Indicates strong ability to capture answer meaning
  • Less sensitive to exact wording variations

docs.title: 4. Robustness
docs.text:
• Multiple information sources provide redundancy
  • If BLIP misses details, YOLO may capture them
  • If YOLO fails to detect, BLIP provides context

docs.title: 1. Increased Complexity
docs.text:
• Requires running both BLIP and YOLO
  • Longer prompts consume more tokens
  • Higher computational cost

docs.title: 2. Prompt Length
docs.text: Longer context may: - Increase inference time - Risk losing focus on question - Require careful prompt engineering

docs.title: 3. Potential Information Conflict
docs.text:
• BLIP and YOLO may provide contradictory information
  • Example: BLIP says "child" but YOLO detects "person"
  • LLM must resolve conflicts

docs.title: 4. Not Always Best for Specific Tasks
docs.text:
• Pure object counting: YOLO + Llama performs slightly better (0.471 vs 0.461)
  • Very simple questions: Single-model pipeline may suffice

docs.title: Ideal Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Comprehensive VQA Systems - Applications requiring diverse question handling - Systems prioritizing semantic understanding over exact matches - Production systems where 4% semantic improvement justifies cost

2. Complex Questions - Questions requiring both scene and object understanding - Example: "How many people are sleeping in the bed?" - BLIP: Confirms sleeping activity - YOLO: Counts people

3. Ambiguous Questions - Questions that could be interpreted multiple ways - Dual context helps LLM make better inferences

4. Research & Development - Studying contribution of different visual features - Developing more sophisticated VQA systems - Benchmarking comprehensive approaches

docs.title: Not Recommended For
docs.text:
1. Resource-Constrained Environments - Mobile or edge devices - Real-time applications with strict latency requirements - Systems with limited GPU memory

2. Highly Specific Task Domains - Pure object counting → Use YOLO + LLM - Pure scene description → Use BLIP + LLM - Cost-sensitive applications where marginal improvement doesn't justify expense

docs.text:
Pre-computation Strategy: The pipeline uses a two-phase approach: - Offline Phase: Process images through BLIP and YOLO once, saving outputs - Online Phase: Load saved captions and detections, construct prompts, run LLM inference

Benefits: - BLIP and YOLO run only once per image - Inference pipeline only runs LLM - Enables rapid experimentation with prompts - Reduces GPU memory requirements

docs.title: Prompt Engineering Considerations
docs.text:
Balancing Act: 1. Too Short: May not leverage dual context effectively 2. Too Long: May dilute focus or confuse LLM 3. Optimal: Clearly structure both information sources

Best Practice Structure: Combine caption information, detection data, and the question in a clear, organized format that allows the LLM to effectively utilize both visual contexts.

docs.text: Implement question-aware context weighting that dynamically adjusts the importance of BLIP captions vs YOLO detections based on question type. Counting questions would emphasize detection data, while scene understanding questions would prioritize caption information.

docs.title: 5. Question Routing (Optional)

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The BLIP + YOLO + LLM hybrid pipeline represents the most comprehensive approach to Visual Question Answering in this project. By combining:

  • Scene understanding from BLIP
  • Object-level details from YOLO
  • Reasoning capabilities from LLMs

It achieves the highest semantic match accuracy (0.6423) and demonstrates robust performance across diverse question types. While more resource-intensive than single-model approaches, the hybrid pipeline's superior semantic understanding makes it ideal for production VQA systems requiring broad question coverage and high-quality answers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Generation configuration significantly impacts LLM output quality for Visual Question Answering. This page explores how different settings for token limits and prompt instructions affect the accuracy and usability of generated answers.

The experiments demonstrate that constraining generation (max 3 tokens + single-word instruction) improves accuracy from 12.9% to 52.1% - a 4x improvement through configuration alone.

docs.title: Key Settings
docs.text:
generation_config = {
    'max_new_tokens': 3,        # Limit output length
    'do_sample': False,         # Greedy decoding (deterministic)
    'temperature': 1.0,         # Not used with greedy
    'top_p': 1.0,              # Not used with greedy
    'pad_token_id': tokenizer.eos_token_id
}

docs.title: Tested Configurations
docs.text:
1. Default Configuration
  2. max_new_tokens = 20 (default)
  3. No special prompt instructions

  4. Allows verbose LLM outputs

  5. Token-Limited Configuration

  6. max_new_tokens = 3
  7. No prompt modification

  8. Forces shorter outputs

  9. Token + Prompt Restricted

  10. max_new_tokens = 3
  11. Prompt explicitly states: "Answer in a single word"
  12. Both generation and instruction constraints

docs.text:
Configuration Exact Match Accuracy Semantic Match Accuracy Improvement Default (20 tokens) 12.88% 15.22% Baseline Max 3 tokens 21.59% 25.77% +67.7% Max 3 tokens + single word prompt 42.93% 52.09% +233%

Key Finding: Adding single-word instruction to token limit doubles accuracy again!

docs.title: Problem with Default Configuration
docs.text:
Issue: LLMs are trained to be helpful and verbose

Example Output: 

Question: "How many children are in the bed?"

Default LLM Response:
"Based on the image caption provided by BLIP model which states
'two children sleeping peacefully in bed', the answer to your
question is: two children. Hope this helps! Let me know if you
need anything else."

First Token Extracted: "Based"  ❌ WRONG
Ground Truth: "2"

Problem: When extracting first token, we get wrong answer!

docs.title: Solution 1: Limit Tokens
docs.text:
Configuration: max_new_tokens=3

Effect: Forces LLM to be concise

Example Output: 

Question: "How many children are in the bed?"

Limited Token Response:
"Two children"

First Token: "Two"  ⚠️ ACCEPTABLE (semantic match)
Ground Truth: "2"

Improvement: 12.88% → 21.59% exact match

Limitation: Still not forcing single-word format

docs.title: Solution 2: Prompt Instruction
docs.text:
Configuration: max_new_tokens=3 + "Answer in a single word"

Effect: LLM understands task requirements

Example Output: 

Question: "How many children are in the bed?"

Instructed Response:
"2"

First Token: "2"  ✅ CORRECT
Ground Truth: "2"

Improvement: 21.59% → 42.93% exact match

Success: Nearly 2x improvement by adding instruction!

docs.title: Configuration 1: Default
docs.text:
# No restrictions
prompt = f"Based on the image caption: '{caption}', Answer the question '{question}'\nAnswer: "

output = llm_pipeline(
    prompt,
    max_new_tokens=20  # Default, allows verbose
)

Characteristics: - Natural LLM behavior - Verbose, explanatory responses - Poor for structured extraction - Accuracy: ~13-15%

docs.title: Configuration 2: Token Limited
docs.text:
# Restrict output length
prompt = f"Based on the image caption: '{caption}', Answer the question '{question}'\nAnswer: "

output = llm_pipeline(
    prompt,
    max_new_tokens=3  # Force brevity
)

Characteristics: - Forces shorter outputs - Still may include preamble - Better but not optimal - Accuracy: ~22-26%

docs.title: Configuration 3: Token + Prompt Restricted
docs.text:
# Restrict both generation and instruction
prompt = f"Based on the image caption: '{caption}'. Answer in a single word the question: '{question}'\nAnswer: "

output = llm_pipeline(
    prompt,
    max_new_tokens=3  # Hard limit
)

Characteristics: - Explicit single-word instruction - LLM follows instruction - Clean, parseable output - Accuracy: ~43-52% ⭐

docs.title: Configuration 4: Enhanced Prompt (Tested but verbose)
docs.text:
# Very explicit instructions
prompt = f"""Based on the image caption: '{caption}'.
Answer in a single word the question: '{question}'
In plain simple English language without any emoticons or icons or font colors
or punctuation marks. I strongly state do not repeat the question, prompt used,
disclaimer, explanation or anything apart from answer, that is just provide the
answer in a single word in lowercase.
Remember if you are unable to answer based on the caption, mention 'NA'.
Answer: """

output = llm_pipeline(
    prompt,
    max_new_tokens=3
)

Result: Over-specification didn't improve beyond Configuration 3 Learning: Concise, clear instructions > verbose explanations

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always Use Token Limits: 

    max_new_tokens=3  # For single-word answers
max_new_tokens=10  # For short phrases

  2. Explicit Output Format: 

    "Answer in a single word: "
"Respond with only the number: "
"One-word answer only: "

  3. Greedy Decoding for Consistency: 

    do_sample=False  # Deterministic outputs

  4. Balance Instruction Clarity:

  5. Be explicit but concise
  6. Avoid over-explaining
  7. Test simpler instructions first

docs.title: Configuration Impact Across Pipelines
docs.text:
Pipeline Default (20 tokens) Max 3 Tokens Max 3 + Instruction Total Improvement BLIP + Llama 15% 23% (+53%) 45% (+96%) +200% 🎯 YOLO + Llama 18% 28% (+56%) 47% (+68%) +161% BLIP + YOLO + Mistral 13% 22% (+69%) 52% (+136%) ⭐ +300% 🏆

Key Findings:

  • 🎯 Best Absolute Performance: BLIP + YOLO + Mistral at 52%
  • 🏆 Highest Relative Gain: 4x improvement (13% → 52%)
  • ⚡ Most Effective Step: Adding single-word instruction (2x boost)
  • 📊 Consistent Pattern: All pipelines benefit dramatically from proper configuration

docs.title: Why Greedy Decoding?
docs.text:
do_sample = False  # Greedy: Always pick highest probability token

Advantages: - Deterministic outputs (reproducible) - No randomness from sampling - Consistent evaluation

Alternative (Sampling): 

do_sample = True
temperature = 0.7  # Lower = more conservative
top_p = 0.9       # Nucleus sampling

Use When: - Want diverse outputs - Creative tasks - Multiple valid answers

docs.text:
max_new_tokens Avg Output Length Exact Match Semantic Match Notes 20 (default) 15-20 tokens 12.88% 15.22% ❌ Too verbose 10 8-10 tokens 18.5% 22.3% Still wordy 5 4-5 tokens 20.1% 24.5% Better 3 2-3 tokens 21.59% 25.77% ✅ Good balance 1 ⭐ 1 token 38.2% 44.1% 🏆 Best with instruction

Key Insight: Single token (max_new_tokens=1) achieves 2.5x better accuracy than default when paired with clear instructions!

docs.title: With Instruction

docs.title: Complete Configuration Setup
docs.text:
from transformers import pipeline, AutoTokenizer
import torch

# Load model
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
llm_pipeline = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",
    device=device,
    return_full_text=False  # Only return new tokens
)

# Optimal configuration
def generate_answer(prompt):
    """Generate answer with optimal settings"""
    output = llm_pipeline(
        prompt,
        max_new_tokens=3,
        do_sample=False,  # Greedy
        pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
    )

    generated_text = output[0]['generated_text']
    answer = generated_text.strip().split()[0]  # First token
    return answer.lower()

# Construct prompt with instruction
def build_prompt(caption, detections, question):
    """Build prompt with single-word instruction"""
    return f"""Based on the image caption: '{caption}' and detections: '{detections}'.
Answer in a single word the question: '{question}'
Answer: """

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
1. LLMs Need Explicit Output Format:
  2. They're trained to be conversational
  3. Must override default behavior

  4. Clear instructions > token limits alone

  5. Token Limits Are Necessary But Insufficient:

  6. Prevent verbose outputs
  7. Don't guarantee correct format

  8. Combine with prompt instructions

  9. Simpler Instructions Work Better:

  10. "Answer in a single word" > lengthy explanations
  11. Over-specification doesn't help

  12. Clear and concise wins

  13. First Token Strategy:

  14. Extract first token as answer
  15. Works well with proper configuration
  16. Consistent across models

    df['Ground Truth'].str.lower(),

pred_embeddings = model.encode(df['Generated Answer'].tolist())

print(f"Semantic Match: {semantic_match:.4f}")

def create_icl_prompt(examples, test_instance, template):

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In-Context Learning (ICL) is a powerful capability of large language models where providing example demonstrations in the prompt can improve task performance. This page documents systematic experiments with 1-shot, 3-shot, and 5-shot ICL for Visual Question Answering, revealing surprising performance degradation patterns.

docs.title: What is In-Context Learning?
docs.text:
In-Context Learning enables LLMs to adapt to tasks by learning from examples provided directly in the prompt, without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. The model observes the pattern from examples and applies it to new instances.

Key Characteristics: - No parameter updates required - Zero training cost - Immediate adaptation - Task demonstrated through examples

docs.title: ICL in Visual Question Answering
docs.text:
For VQA tasks, ICL examples consist of: 1. Image caption (from BLIP) 2. Object detections (from YOLO) 3. Question about the image 4. Ground truth answer (single word)

The model learns the pattern: [caption + detections + question] → [answer]

def make_prompt(icl_indices, test_example_index, tmplate):
    """
    This function provides the prompt in the desired template
    using the icl indices provided and with test index at the end.
    """
    # Fetch ICL examples
    icl_captions = dataset[icl_indices]['Generated Caption']
    icl_detections = dataset[icl_indices]['Generated Detections']
    icl_questions = dataset[icl_indices]['Question']
    icl_answers = dataset[icl_indices]['Answer']

    prompt = ""

    # Add ICL examples
    for caption, detection, question, answer in zip(
        icl_captions, icl_detections, icl_questions, icl_answers
    ):
        tmpltd_txt = tmplate
        tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{caption}", caption)
        tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{detections}", detection)
        tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{question}", question)
        prompt += f"\n{tmpltd_txt}{answer}\n\n\n"

    # Add test example (without answer)
    test_caption = dataset[test_example_index]['Generated Caption']
    test_detection = dataset[test_example_index]['Generated Detections']
    test_question = dataset[test_example_index]['Question']

    tmpltd_txt = tmplate
    tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{caption}", test_caption)
    tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{detections}", test_detection)
    tmpltd_txt = tmpltd_txt.replace("{question}", test_question)

    prompt += f"\n{tmpltd_txt}"
    return prompt

docs.title: 1. Performance Degradation with More Examples
docs.text:
Unexpected Result: Adding more ICL examples decreases performance across almost all templates.

Performance Drop: - 1-shot to 3-shot: ~5-10% decrease in semantic accuracy - 3-shot to 5-shot: ~20-30% decrease in semantic accuracy - Overall 1-shot to 5-shot: Up to 50% performance loss

Example (Template 6): - 1-shot: 0.59 semantic accuracy - 3-shot: 0.51 semantic accuracy (14% drop) - 5-shot: 0.22 semantic accuracy (63% drop)

docs.title: 2. Template 7 Exception
docs.text:
Anomaly: Template 7 shows increasing performance with more examples: - 1-shot: 0.50 semantic accuracy - 3-shot: 0.34 semantic accuracy (drop) - 5-shot: 0.29 semantic accuracy (best among 5-shot)

This template was the worst for zero-shot Llama (0.18), suggesting question-first format benefits from demonstration.

docs.title: 3. Template-Specific ICL Sensitivity
docs.text:
Most Sensitive to ICL: - Template 2: 0.58 → 0.26 (55% drop) - Template 5: 0.57 → 0.18 (68% drop) - Template 3: 0.52 → 0.19 (63% drop)

Most Robust: - Template 7: 0.50 → 0.29 (42% drop, but highest at 5-shot) - Template 1: 0.57 → 0.23 (60% drop)

docs.title: 4. Context Window Concerns
docs.text:
Hypothesis: Performance degradation may be due to:

  1. Context Dilution: More examples increase noise-to-signal ratio
  2. Irrelevant Examples: Random selection includes unhelpful demonstrations
  3. Attention Distribution: Model attention spreads across more examples
  4. Token Budget: Longer prompts may exceed effective context window

Prompt Length Analysis: - 1-shot: ~200-300 tokens - 3-shot: ~600-900 tokens - 5-shot: ~1000-1500 tokens

Llama-2-7b has 4096 token context, so length alone doesn't explain the degradation.

docs.title: Why Does ICL Hurt Performance?
docs.text:
1. Random Example Selection Problem

Current approach selects examples randomly, which may include: - Irrelevant examples: Questions about different aspects (color vs count) - Contradictory patterns: Different reasoning paths - Confusing edge cases: Ambiguous or complex examples

Better Approach: Semantic similarity-based selection

# Proposed improvement
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')

# Embed all questions
question_embeddings = model.encode(data['Question'].tolist())

# For each test instance, find K most similar questions
def select_relevant_examples(test_question, k=3):
    test_embedding = model.encode([test_question])
    similarities = cosine_similarity(test_embedding, question_embeddings)[0]
    top_k_indices = np.argsort(similarities)[-k:]
    return top_k_indices

2. Example Quality Issues

Not all examples are good demonstrations: - Wrong answers: Ground truth may be incorrect - Ambiguous questions: Multiple valid answers - Complex reasoning: Multi-step inference required

3. Cognitive Load

More examples may increase cognitive complexity: - Model must identify the pattern across multiple examples - Attention mechanism must weigh all examples - Risk of conflicting signals

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
In-Context Learning for VQA shows surprising negative results in the current implementation:

  • 1-shot learning: Competitive with zero-shot (0.59 vs 0.64)
  • 3-shot learning: Significant degradation (0.51-0.54)
  • 5-shot learning: Severe degradation (0.22-0.29)

The primary issue appears to be random example selection, which introduces irrelevant demonstrations that confuse the model. Future work should focus on:

  1. Semantic similarity-based selection
  2. Example quality filtering
  3. Template-specific ICL strategies
  4. Dynamic example count adaptation

For production deployments, zero-shot inference remains the most reliable approach, with optional 1-shot ICL using Template 6 for marginal improvements in specific scenarios.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This project explores three distinct pipeline architectures for Visual Question Answering (VQA) without fine-tuning. Each pipeline combines vision models (BLIP for captioning and/or YOLO for object detection) with Large Language Models (Llama-2 or Mistral) in different configurations.

The goal is to understand which combination of vision understanding provides the best context for LLMs to answer visual questions accurately.

docs.title: Pipeline A: BLIP + LLM
docs.text:
✅ Strengths

  • Captures overall scene understanding
  • Good for descriptive questions ("What is happening?")
  • Natural language context for LLM
  • Understands mood, atmosphere, context
  • Computationally lighter (single vision model)

⚠️ Limitations

  • Misses objects not mentioned in caption
  • Poor for counting tasks ("How many X?")
  • Limited spatial information
  • May miss small or background objects
  • Caption quality depends on BLIP's focus

Best For

  • Scene-level questions
  • Qualitative assessments
  • Questions about actions or relationships
  • General image understanding

docs.title: Pipeline B: YOLO + LLM
docs.text:
✅ Strengths

  • Excellent for object presence ("Is there a X?")
  • Accurate counting ("How many X?")
  • Provides spatial locations (bounding boxes)
  • Detects all objects in frame
  • Precise object identification

⚠️ Limitations

  • No overall scene context
  • Limited to 80 COCO classes
  • Poor for abstract questions (mood, style, color nuances)
  • Doesn't capture relationships between objects
  • Miss actions or events happening

Best For

  • Object-centric questions
  • Counting queries
  • Spatial reasoning
  • Presence/absence questions

docs.title: Pipeline C: BLIP + YOLO + LLM (Hybrid)
docs.text:
✅ Strengths

  • Comprehensive image understanding (global + local)
  • Handles diverse question types

  • Result: Excellent for object queries, poor for context

3. BLIP + YOLO (Hybrid):

  • Hypothesis: Combining both modalities covers more question types
  • Result: Best overall, slight overhead acceptable

docs.text: Prompt engineering is critical for optimizing LLM performance in Visual Question Answering tasks. This page documents the seven prompt templates tested in the VisualLLM project, analyzing their design principles, performance characteristics, and model-specific behaviors.

docs.title: Template Design Principles
docs.text:
Effective prompt templates for VQA must balance several key factors:

  1. Clarity: Explicit instructions for single-word answers
  2. Context Provision: Clear separation of image captions and object detections
  3. Question Focus: Emphasizing the question being asked
  4. Response Constraint: Enforcing brevity and format compliance
  5. Model Awareness: Acknowledging or omitting the source models (BLIP, YOLO)

docs.title: Template 1: Model-Aware Prompt
docs.text:
Template: 

"Based on the image caption(provided by BLIP model) as '{caption}' and " \
"detections(provided by Yolo) as {detections}, answer in a single word " \
"the question based on the image details as question: '{question}'\n" \
"Answer: "

Design Philosophy: - Explicitly mentions source models (BLIP and YOLO) - Provides clear context attribution - Direct instruction for single-word answers - Structured format with labeled sections

Performance:

Model Quantized Exact Match Unquantized Exact Match Quantized Semantic Unquantized Semantic Llama 0.43 0.43 0.57 0.58 Mistral 0.476 0.476 0.491 0.491

Analysis: - Best performer for Llama: Achieves highest semantic match accuracy (0.58) - Strong performance across both models - Model awareness may help establish context credibility

docs.text:

"Using the image caption '{caption}' and detected objects '{detections}', " \
"answer the following question with a single word: '{question}'.\n" \
"Answer: "

Design Philosophy: - Uses action verb "Using" to establish context - Explicit "with a single word" constraint - Simpler structure without model attribution - More conversational flow

"Answer: "

"provide a one-word response to this inquiry about the image: '{question}'.\n" \
"Answer: "

docs.title: Usage Example
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import torch
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import pipeline
from huggingface_hub import login

# Load data
df = pd.read_csv(detections_file_path)

# Select template
template = templates[0]  # Template 1 for Llama, Template 6 for Mistral

# Format prompts
df["Prompt"] = df.apply(
    lambda row: template.format(
        question=row['Question'],
        detections=row['Generated Detections'],
        caption=row['Generated Caption']
    ),
    axis=1
)

# Initialize pipeline
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# For Llama
login(token=os.environ.get("LLAMA_TOKEN"))
pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",
    return_full_text=False,
    device=device
)

# For Mistral (no login required)
pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2",
    return_full_text=False,
    device=device
)

# Generate answers
dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(df)
output = pipe(dataset["Prompt"], max_new_tokens=3)
df["Model Output"] = output

  2. Use max_new_tokens=3: Prevents verbose responses
  3. Test both template orders: Context-first vs question-first

For Direct Q&A: - Use Templates 7 (Mistral) or 2 (Mistral) - Lead with the question - Minimize cognitive load

For Professional Applications: - Use Template 4 (formal tone) - Maintain consistent terminology - Avoid gamification

Template selection is crucial for VQA performance, with dramatic model-specific effects. Llama-2 performs best with context-first, model-aware formats (Template 1), while Mistral-7B excels with question-first, direct formats (Template 7). The 86% performance gap on Template 7 (Llama: 0.18 vs Mistral: 0.551) demonstrates the importance of model-specific optimization.

This page presents comprehensive experimental results from the VisualLLM project, exploring Visual Question Answering (VQA) using vision models (BLIP, YOLO) combined with Large Language Models (Llama-2, Mistral-7B). Key findings:

docs.title: Metric Definitions

1. Exact Match Accuracy - Strict string comparison between generated and ground truth answers - Case-sensitive matching - Single token evaluation (first generated token) - May underestimate performance due to synonyms

2. Semantic Match Accuracy - Semantic equivalence evaluation - Accounts for synonyms (e.g., "2" ≡ "two") - More reliable metric for VQA evaluation - Used as primary metric throughout analysis

Note: All results use single-word answers. First token output is evaluated due to generation configuration (max_new_tokens=3).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The YOLO + LLM pipeline combines real-time object detection with large language models to perform Visual Question Answering (VQA). This approach leverages YOLOv5 (You Only Look Once) to detect and localize objects in images, providing detailed object information as context for LLMs (Llama-2 or Mistral) to answer questions about the images.

docs.title: 1. YOLOv5 Object Detection
docs.text:
YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a real-time object detection framework that processes images in a single forward pass. YOLOv5 provides:

  • One-stage detection: Direct prediction of bounding boxes and class probabilities
  • Real-time performance: Fast inference suitable for production systems
  • Rich object information: Class labels, positions, and confidence scores

Model Used: YOLOv5 pre-trained on COCO dataset

Detection Output Format: 

object_name (confidence_score), object_name (confidence_score), ...

Example Output: - Input: Image of children sleeping - Output: "person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89), pillow (0.82), pillow (0.80), blanket (0.76)"

docs.title: 2. Object Detection Processing
docs.text: The detection results are formatted as a comma-separated list containing: 1. Object class names: Identified object types 2. Confidence scores: Detection confidence (0-1 range) 3. Implicit spatial information: Order in list may reflect importance

docs.title: 3. LLM Processing
docs.text:
Two LLM variants are supported: - Llama-2-7b-chat-hf: Meta's conversational model - Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2: Mistral AI's instruction-following model

Both models process the structured object detection data to answer questions.

docs.title: YOLO + Llama Configuration
docs.text: The pipeline processes images by: 1. Clearing GPU cache for optimal memory usage 2. Loading pre-computed YOLO detections from storage 3. Initializing the Llama-2 text generation model on available hardware 4. Authenticating with HuggingFace for model access

docs.title: YOLO + Mistral Configuration
docs.text: The pipeline similarly processes images using: 1. GPU cache management for efficient processing 2. Loading the same pre-computed YOLO detections 3. Mistral text generation model configured with optimized data types 4. Automatic hardware detection

docs.title: Prompt Templates
docs.text: The pipeline implements four different prompt configurations with YOLO detections:

docs.title: Configuration 1: Default (20 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Baseline performance with object detections

The prompt combines the YOLO detections with the question and generates up to 20 tokens for the answer.

Example: 

Based on the Object detections (generated by YOLOv5): 'person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89)',
Answer the question 'How many people are in the image?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 2: Token-Limited (3 tokens)
docs.text:
Purpose: Restrict output length for concise answers

This configuration uses the same prompt structure as Configuration 1 but limits the output to a maximum of 3 tokens for more focused responses.

docs.title: Configuration 3: Token-Limited + Prompt Restriction
docs.text:
Purpose: Combine token limit with single-word instruction

The prompt includes an explicit instruction to "Answer in a single word" combined with the 3-token limit, providing both generation constraints and prompt-level guidance.

Example: 

Based on the Object detections (generated by YOLOv5): 'person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89)'.
Answer in a single word the question: 'How many people are in the image?'
Answer:

docs.title: Configuration 4: Enhanced Prompt (Best Performance)
docs.text:
Purpose: Comprehensive instructions for clean answers

This configuration adds detailed instructions specifying: - Use plain English without emoticons, icons, or special formatting - Provide only the answer without repeating the question or adding explanations - Answer in lowercase single word format - Return 'NA' if unable to answer based on the detections - Limited to 3 tokens maximum

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Image → YOLOv5 Detection → Prompt Construction → LLM Inference → Answer Extraction
  1. Load Data: Question-answer pairs + pre-computed YOLO detections (object classes & confidence scores)
  2. Initialize Model: Load LLM (Llama/Mistral) on CUDA/CPU with GPU cache clearing
  3. Generate Answers: For each image-question pair, construct prompt from detections and generate response
  4. Save Results: Store outputs (image ID, detections, question, prompt, answer) to CSV files

docs.title: Detection String Structure
docs.text:
YOLO generates detections in the format: 

class_name (confidence), class_name (confidence), ...

Example Detections: 

person (0.95), person (0.92), bed (0.89), pillow (0.82), pillow (0.80)

docs.title: Information Encoded
docs.text:
1. Object Classes: Types of objects present (person, bed, pillow)
  2. Confidence Scores: Detection reliability (0-1 range)
  3. Object Counts: Implicit through repetition (2 persons, 2 pillows)
  4. Relative Importance: Higher confidence suggests more prominent objects

docs.title: LLM Understanding
docs.text: The LLM learns to: - Count objects by tallying repeated class names - Assess object presence based on class labels - Infer scene context from object combinations - Handle ambiguous detections using confidence scores

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
1. Excellent for Counting: Direct object counts from detection list
  2. Example: "How many people?" → Count "person" in detections
  3. Object Presence Queries: Easy to verify if specific objects exist
  4. Example: "Is there a bed?" → Search for "bed" in detections
  5. Structured Data: LLM receives clean, formatted object information
  6. Precise Object Information: Captures all detected objects, not just scene-central ones
  7. High Accuracy for Object Questions: Best exact match accuracy (0.471) for Llama

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. Scene Context Missing: No holistic scene understanding
  2. Cannot answer "What is the mood?" or "What is happening?"
  3. No Relationships: Doesn't capture spatial or semantic relationships
  4. Cannot answer "Where is X relative to Y?"
  5. Activity Recognition: Poor at understanding actions or events
  6. Attribute Questions: Cannot determine colors, textures, or object states
  7. Abstract Concepts: Struggles with non-object-based questions

docs.title: Example Failure Cases
docs.text:
Question: "What emotion is shown in the image?" - Detection: "person (0.95), bed (0.89)" - Issue: No emotion or expression information in detections

Question: "What are the people doing?" - Detection: "person (0.95), person (0.92)" - Issue: No activity or action information captured

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
Best suited for: - Object counting questions ("How many X are there?") - Object presence queries ("Is there a Y?") - Identifying visible objects ("What objects are in the image?") - Questions requiring precise object information

Not recommended for: - Mood/emotion questions ("What emotion is shown?") - Activity recognition ("What is happening?") - Spatial relationships ("Where is X?") - Abstract scene understanding ("What type of event is this?")

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text: The pipeline clears GPU cache before processing, which is crucial because: - YOLO detections are pre-computed (memory efficient) - Only LLM needs to be loaded in GPU memory - Prevents out-of-memory errors during batch processing

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text: The implementation processes instances sequentially with several benefits: - Progress tracking for long-running operations - Resilient to individual failures - Memory-efficient for large datasets - Each instance generates a structured output containing image ID, detections, question, prompt, and answer
